transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-12 16:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Nina (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Jules (Redwood CSM), Samir (Aurora Platform Lead), Laura (Aurora SRE), Mike (Aurora Product), Priya (Aurora ML)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to align on benchmark acceptance criteria, harness integration for customer scripts, and streaming vs non-streaming paths. Goal: run a 6-hour benchmark across hosted/dedicated configs and validate latency p95/p99, throughput, and cost per 1M tokens.

Topics discussed:
- Workload sizing (QPS, bursts, seq length)
- Streaming vs non-streaming probe and fallthrough routing
- Harness adapter: customer script shapes and example integration points
- Success criteria: latency percentile targets, error rate, stability window
- Timeline and next steps for bench run and post-mortem

Transcript body:
[00:00] Nina (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, um let's maybe do quick intros then jump to the workloads Samir can you start with what you're trying to validate in this poc
[00:18] Samir (Aurora): yeah hi all, Samir here. high level: Aurora's chat summarization infra needs to serve realtime clinical summarization. We care about tail latency and determinism — 95th under 220ms for streaming responses and 99th under 400ms for non-streaming full-response calls. Our current infra is a mixed vcluster of G4/RTX and some colocation A100s. we want to know if Redwood can hit these numbers at scale and how to plug our existing request generator into your harness.
[00:45] Marco (Redwood SE): cool, thanks. just to clarify the acceptance windows you mentioned — p95 < 220ms streaming and p99 < 400ms batch/full response — those are end-to-end from client to final chunk visible to user?
[01:05] Samir: yes, from client TCP e2e — includes network to the region, inference time and chunking overhead.
[01:18] Priya (Aurora ML): i also want to see model quality parity, but for the bench phase we can do functional checks with a curated prompt set. if latency/compliance is ok we'll do a small quality run later.
[01:35] Nina: great. Laura, can you share the traffic profile quickly?
[01:40] Laura (Aurora SRE): sure — baseline steady 120 qps, 20% of requests are long sequences (avg 512 tokens), typical request size 80 tokens, bursts to 450 qps for a 10-15 minute window in mornings. error budget is 0.5% per hour.
[01:58] Mike (Product): and our SLAs are user-facing so we need deterministic cold start behavior — ideally cold-start tail should not exceed 1s additional to warm.
[02:12] Marco: ok that helps. on Redwood side we'll provision a harness run that exercises both streaming (SSE/chunked) and non-streaming (single response) paths. question: do you prefer us to replay your real traffic (we can accept traces) or run generated synthetic scripts?
[02:35] Samir: we can provide traces but we also want to run our in-proc python client that handles our prompt templating. that script uses long-lived HTTP connections and SSE. it's not standard bench tooling but we can adapt it.
[02:50] Marco: perfect — that's actually helpful. we'll write a small adapter that wraps your script to talk to Redwood's harness endpoint; typically we add a thin shim to emit the right headers and capture chunk latencies. we have an example repo.
[03:08] Jules (CSM): to avoid surprises we should capture token-per-second, per-chunk latency, p50/p95/p99 per-endpoint, 5xx rates and KVCACHE hit rates if available.
[03:26] Priya: what's kv cache metrics? we currently rely on our own Redis-based prefix cache but we'd like to see Redwood's KV cache warmup impact
[03:33] Marco: right, Redwood runtime exposes kv_cache_hit_rate and token_generation_ms per-call in the bench telemetry. small note: transcription here might show KV cahce typo in logs ;).
[03:47] Laura: for the harness run we need to know what sequence of runs you recommend — warm-up, steady-state, and stress spike?
[03:55] Marco: recommended plan: 15-min warmup at 50% baseline, 2-hour steady-state at baseline 120 qps, 30-minute spike to 450 qps, 1-hour recovery at baseline, then 2-hour long-run to validate stability. totals ~6 hours. we can shorten if you want.
[04:15] Samir: OK. How do you handle streaming vs non-streaming routing? we sometimes want streaming for interactive clients and non-streaming for batch jobs.
[04:25] Nina: Redwood supports per-route streaming flags; the harness can alternate routes or run parallel routes. also we can test fallthrough routing: if model variant A can't keep up we fall back to A-quantized or smaller LLM to preserve latency SLOs. we'll show cost delta for fallbacks.
[04:45] Mike: how do you simulate client-side backpressure? our client cancels mid-stream sometimes and we need to measure server CPU/connection leak behaviour.
[04:55] Marco: our adapter will replay your client cancel events; we recommend adding a churn test with 1% early cancels replicated during the spike window. us to capture open socket counts and goroutine leaks; for private deployment we can also run strace-level metrics if needed.
[05:12] Samir: what hardware will be used in the dedicated run? we have a mix but for apples-to-apples we want A100-80GB vs your hosted instance.
[05:21] Marco: bench will run on a dedicated A100-80GB rack by default; we can run an additional hosted run on our multi-tenant fleet for contrast. we'll record device utilization and per-GPU token/s.
[05:36] Priya: cost visibility: we need tokens-per-dollar breakdown and also per-route cost when fallback occurs.
[05:44] Jules: yep, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and cost delta for fallbacks plus a breakdown by model variant and quantization profile. we'll include a sample dashboard.
[05:56] Laura: security/regulatory: this POC must run in our VPC with KMS-managed keys for logs. can Redwood run the bench in our VPC or do we need Private deployment?
[06:10] Nina: for benchmarks we can either run the harness in your VPC via Private deployment image, or run hosted and stream telemetry over a secure pipeline. given you need KMS for logs we recommend Private bench in your VPC; that will require a short onboard (VPC peering or transit). we'll include the SOC2 notes.
[06:27] Mike: timeline — we want results before end of month. is that realistic?
[06:33] Marco: yes if we get scripts and traces within 48 hours we can schedule the bench next week and deliver a results deck within 48 hours post-run.
[06:43] Samir: success criteria recap: 1) p95 streaming < 220ms, p99 non-streaming < 400ms; 2) error rate < 0.5% during steady-state; 3) no memory leaks during churn; 4) cost per 1M tokens below our internal threshold (Priya will share).
[07:03] Priya: we also want reproducible harness runs — seed control and deterministic prompt ordering so we can compare quality runs across models.
[07:12] Marco: we'll expose run ids and a seed-controlled runner so you can re-run same workload.
[07:20] Laura: what about streaming fallback behavior — if we route to smaller quantized model mid-stream is there risk of incoherent partial responses?
[07:30] Marco: good question. Redwood fallback is at request granularity; we don't mid-stream migrate a single request to another model. instead if a model is overloaded subsequent requests are routed to fallback. for live sessions we can implement an early-fallback heuristic that returns faster but with possible shorter completions. we'll demo both behaviors in the bench.
[07:52] Samir: anything we should avoid in our scripts to make the harness happy?
[07:58] Marco: avoid bespoke binary protocols, keep HTTP chunking standard, and include a small json meta header on each request so the adapter can map logs back to your trace ids. also make sure your client exposes per-chunk timestamps.
[08:14] Nina: we'll share a short adapter example repo link in the follow-up (Link: https://redwood.example.com/harness-adapters/aurora-sample).
[08:24] Mike: whats the expected resource ramp? like if we run the spike will you auto-scale?
[08:30] Marco: for dedicated bench we can pin GPUs and simulate oversubscribe; for hosted ramp we'll show autoscale behavior and then a reserved run on Dedicated to show predictable latency under reserved capacity. important for your SLOs.
[08:43] Priya: do you support quantized variants and measuring quality regression?
[08:47] Marco: yes — Redwood Optimize will run a quick eval on the response set for quantized models and report BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics against your reference set. this will be part of the bench report.
[08:58] Laura: any gotchas on the per-call logging? we require logs to be pushed to our S3 bucket using our KMS keys, ideally obfuscated PII fields.
[09:08] Nina: we have a log delivery option to your S3 with envelope encryption via your KMS. we can also apply PII scrubbing hooks as a pre-delivery step. we'll add that to the runbook.
[09:20] Samir: ok let's recap next steps and owners
[09:25] Nina: recap — Redwood to: 1) send POC runbook and adapter repo, 2) prepare harness adapter example and schedule bench window, 3) provide pricing for dedicated pool and fallback cost estimates. Aurora to: 1) upload two 1-hour traffic traces and the in-proc python script, 2) confirm VPC peering window, 3) send internal cost threshold.
[09:48] Mike: agreed. one more question — will you capture cold-start tail percentiles per model variant?
[09:55] Marco: yes; bench will include cold-start windows with new worker spin-ups and we'll produce per-model cold-start p50/p95/p99.
[10:04] Jules: I'll schedule the 3-hour run and propose time slots, we'll try for next Thursday morning PT.
[10:12] Laura: fine. I'll aim to upload traces by Monday EOD.
[10:18] Nina: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a calendar invite and deliverables.
[10:24] (call ends)
